name: Gastric plication

lead: Gastric plication reduces stomach volume by folding the stomach wall inward and stitching it, rather than cutting out part of it. It is a bariatric (weight-loss) procedure, done laparoscopically or with an endoscope.

Its appearance payoff comes through weight loss: less body fat means a leaner body and often a slimmer face and more visible bone structure. Trials and reviews report weight loss, but a 2018 meta-analysis found sleeve gastrectomy produced greater loss with fewer complications.

paras: It is performed by a surgeon or endoscopist in a clinic or hospital setting as part of a supervised weight-management programme, and is followed by dietary stages and long-term follow-up. Endoscopic variants include techniques such as endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty.

Reported problems include complications, reoperation, inadequate weight loss and, historically, a case report of Wernicke-Korsakoff encephalopathy after plication. Guidelines advise multidisciplinary care with long-term follow-up.

web.title: Effects of Bariatric Surgery on Facial Features

chain: Stomach folded to a smaller volume
Leaner body and face, more visible bone structure
angle.text: Plication is used to lose fat when diet and exercise have not been enough. As body fat falls, features such as the jaw and cheekbones become more visible and the body slimmer.

lead: Gastric plication is a restrictive bariatric procedure in which the stomach is folded inward and sutured to reduce its volume, achieving restriction without stapling, banding or resection [1]. Endoscopic versions use endoluminal sutures and include endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty and the primary obesity surgery endolumenal (POSE) procedure [2].

People interested in appearance come to it for the chain it sets off: smaller stomach, lower food intake, fat loss, then a leaner body and face. Weight loss is the mechanism; the procedure itself does not change facial structure. Because nothing is cut out or removed, Wikipedia describes the stomach being sutured into a sleeve rather than cut and notes that plication is reversible but has less durable weight loss than other operations.

It sits among a family of bariatric operations. Wikipedia lists gastric plication with adjustable bands and balloons, while sleeve gastrectomy and gastric bypass are the most common standard procedures. Its endoscopic cousin, endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty, was authorized by the US FDA in July 2022 for people with a body mass index of 30 to 50, according to Wikipedia's summary [3].

Research consists of case series, small randomised trials, a sham-controlled endoscopic trial and meta-analyses, with the main published comparison finding that sleeve gastrectomy produced greater weight loss and fewer complications than laparoscopic plication [4].

paras: In a feasibility study of laparoscopic plication, the anterior stomach wall was folded inward from the fundus to the antrum with two rows of sutures in one method, with a second method also tested [5]. A surgeon reporting a 12-year personal experience described modifications such as one-row bilateral plication and the question of including or excluding the right gastroepiploic artery [6].

Wikipedia contrasts it with sleeve gastrectomy, where a large portion of the stomach is surgically removed and the operation is not reversible, and with gastric bypass, where a small pouch is connected to the small intestine. Gastric plication leaves the folded stomach in place, which is why it is described as reversible.

A report titled Gastric plication for morbid obesity appeared in the Journal of the Kansas Medical Society in 1976 [7]. A 1982 JAMA report described Wernicke-Korsakoff encephalopathy after gastric plication [8]. Laparoscopic versions were studied from around 2010 [5][6]. Endoscopic approaches such as transoral gastric volume reduction were reported in an 18-patient feasibility study [9].

A 2012 systematic review looked at the laparoscopic literature [10], a 2013 review described how to reduce stomach size without transection [1], and a 2013 report stressed the importance of postoperative follow-up in short-term outcomes [11]. Registered trials from 2009 to 2013 examined plication in people with morbid obesity, in adolescents, and combined with adjustable banding, with one registered banding comparison enrolling 420 people [12][13][14].

Endoscopic plication techniques place sutures through the mouth with a flexible endoscope, so there are no abdominal incisions. A review lists endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty, POSE, transoral gastroplasty and plication using a circular stapler among them, and at the time of that review POSE was under US FDA review and endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty was gaining acceptance [2]. Wikipedia reports that most endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty uses the Apollo device attached to a double-channel endoscope, and that the FDA authorized it in July 2022 for a BMI of 30 to 50 [3].

In the MERIT randomised trial of 209 adults with BMI 30 to 40, summarised on Wikipedia, the endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty group lost about 13.6 percent of body weight at one year versus about 0.8 percent in lifestyle-only controls, and about 80 percent had improvement in at least one obesity-related condition [3]. The same page reports that laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy produced more weight loss in comparisons, that mild to moderate stomach symptoms such as nausea and bloating affect most patients but usually settle within about a week, and that serious complications including bleeding, leak and perforation are reported as rare [3].

A review of endoscopic plication techniques concluded they are effective for weight loss, with potentially higher efficacy than medications and lifestyle change and lower invasiveness than surgery, and recommended use within a multidisciplinary programme with long-term follow-up [2].

A 2018 meta-analysis of 12 studies compared laparoscopic plication with sleeve gastrectomy and found sleeve gastrectomy had lower overall complications and higher percent excess weight loss, with no difference in hospital stay, operative duration, reoperation or cost; the authors called for larger randomised trials [4]. A systematic review of plication for morbid obesity and a randomised trial against mini-gastric bypass have also been published [10][15].

For people pursuing leaner features, the face changes as body fat falls, but the timing and effect vary. A small 2015 prospective study at one US medical centre photographed 14 gastric bypass patients before surgery and three to six months after and asked online survey respondents to rate age and attractiveness from photographs. Post-operative photographs were rated higher on average by 0.256 points on a 10-point scale, and five of the 14 patients showed a statistically significant change in perceived age, three older and two younger. The authors suggested mild weight loss might make patients look younger but less attractive, while large weight loss might look older but more attractive, and they described the sample and design as limited [16].
That study examined gastric bypass, not plication, so it describes bariatric weight loss in general rather than this procedure specifically [16].

The meta-analysis above found a higher overall complication rate for plication than for sleeve gastrectomy [4]. A report on short-term outcomes stresses the importance of postoperative follow-up [11]. Nutritional deficiency complications, including the Wernicke-Korsakoff case report, have been documented [8].

Wikipedia's bariatric surgery summary lists general risks of weight-loss operations including nutritional deficiencies, reflux with some procedures, and low multivitamin adherence, and says contraindications include active ulcer disease, pregnancy, untreated psychiatric conditions and eating disorders. Current consensus criteria cited there recommend considering surgery for adults with BMI above 35, or 30 to 35 with metabolic syndrome, as set out by the ASMBS and IFSO in October 2022.

The ESSENTIAL trial, a randomised sham-controlled study, evaluated endoscopic plication (the POSE procedure) in people with class I to II obesity, with all subjects receiving low-intensity lifestyle therapy; endpoints were percent total body weight loss at 12 months and the share achieving at least 5% [17]. A 2018 meta-analysis of 12 studies compared laparoscopic plication with sleeve gastrectomy and found lower complications and higher excess weight loss with sleeve gastrectomy, with no difference in hospital stay, operative time, reoperation or cost [4]. A randomised trial compared plication with mini-gastric bypass [15], and a systematic review covered plication for morbid obesity [10].

A European guideline's network meta-analysis covered plication among several bariatric options [18]. Registered trials include studies of plication in adolescents, combined with banding, and endoscopic suturing devices [12][19][13][14]. Wikipedia's account of the MERIT trial of endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty reports about 13.6 percent total body weight loss at one year [3].
